rows.title: Accounting with QuickBooks and Excel
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Describe the functions of pre-programmed general ledger accounting package.
Save, retrieve, adjust, correct, and modify data files.
Demonstrate the program's operation and application.
Produce integrated accounting reports.
Apply special functions of the program -depreciation, payroll, inventory.
Read selected reports to determine net income, balances, and variances.
Produce functional spreadsheets.
Write practical mathematical formulas to maximize spreadsheet effectiveness.
Display proper spreadsheet report format.
Interpret special applications and capabilities of Excel spreadsheets.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Identify and record changes in assets, liabilities, and owners' equity.

Complete the steps in the accounting cycle for service and retail merchandising businesses including the following: a) prepare a balance sheet, income statement, and statement of owners' equity; b) determine and define balances of T-accounts having entries recorded on both sides of the account; c) present the fundamental accounting equation with T-account form; d) prepare a trial balance; e) record a group of transactions in a two-column general journal format and post entries; f) complete a worksheet; g) prepare an income statement, a statement of owners' equity, and a balance sheet directly from the worksheet; h) journalize and post adjusting entries and; i) journalize and post closing entries; j) prepare a post-closing trial balance and interim financial statements.
Employ information technology to accomplish the preceding tasks.

rows.title: Introduction to Managerial Accounting
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Students will demonstrate the ability to analyze, record, and post journal entries related to bond transactions.
Students will demonstrate the ability to prepare and analyze a statement of cash flows.
Students will demonstrate the ability to analyze financial statements.

Students will demonstrate the ability to utilize costing systems (process, job order, and activity-based) to accumulate and analyze costs and to explain the components and common behavior patterns of costs.
Students will demonstrate the ability to use accounting information to make decisions using analytical process such as budgets, cost-volume-profit analysis, variance analysis, and capital budgeting.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Identify and illustrate the primary activities and information needs of managers and explain the role of the managerial accountant as a member of the management team.
Compare and contrast financial and managerial accounting.
Define and illustrate various cost terms, concepts, and behaviors, and evaluate their relevancy for various decision-making purposes.
Distinguish between product and period costs.
Prepare traditional and contribution-margin income statements and define the related terms.
Explain cost-volume-profit analysis, degree of operating leverage, and safety margin; employee each as an analytical tool.
Describe and utilize costing systems (process, job order, and activity-based) to accumulate and analyze costs and prepare related accounting records and reports.
Discuss the impact of technology on the business environment, its implications for product and service costs, and the development of activity-based costing.
Explain the purposes of budgeting, prepare a master budget and its component schedules, and relate the budget to planning and control activities.
Explain the development and use of standard costs and flexible budgets, prepare and interpret variance analysis reports and relate them to responsibility accounting and control.
Explain the nature of and need for segment reporting and the relationship with cost, revenue, profit, and investment centers; prepare and analyze related segment reports.
Compare and contrast absorption costing and variable costing, prepare income statements using both methods, and reconcile the resulting net incomes.
Define relevant costs and benefits and prepare analyses related to special decisions.
Explain the nature of capital expenditure decisions and apply and evaluate various methods used in making these decisions, including the time value of money.
Identify the ethical implications inherent in managerial accounting and reporting and be able to apply strategies for addressing them.

rows.title: Essentials of Human Anatomy and Physiology
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Identify gross anatomy of the various systems in the human body.
Describe the structure and function of various histology slides.
Explain physiological processes of the various systems in the human body.
Identify the various parts and proper usage of the light microscope.
Comprehend the overall performance of the human body.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Explain how anatomy and physiology are related.
Explain how the study of the living body is dependent on chemistry and how this relates to homeostasis.
Discuss how pH and its effects on the body relate to physiology.
Describe how cell structure relates to function.
Compare and contrast the four main types of tissue in the body.
Discuss three factors that influence skin color.
Discuss the structure and functions of the glands of the skin.
Discuss the five functions of the skeletal system.
Distinguish between the axial and appendicular skeletons and state the number of bones in each.
Compare the structure and function of the three types of joints.
Compare skeletal muscle tissue with visceral and cardiac muscle tissue.
Describe and discuss the microscopic structure and function of the muscle cell.
Describe and discuss the neurological and physiological interaction of muscles.
Discuss the origin and insertion and action of major muscle groups.
Compare and contrast the CNS, PNS, and ANS.
Describe membrane potentials and the events of impulse conduction.
Compare and contrast the actions of the endocrine and nervous system.
Explain how the blood levels of hormones are regulated.
Describe the location, hormones, and functions of the endocrine glands.
Explain where and how blood is produced.
Compare and contrast WBC structure and function.
Describe mechanical and physiological functions of the heart.
Analyze the factors that affect heart rate.
Compare and contrast pulse rate and blood pressure.
Explain and describe the parts of the lymphatic system and their functions in maintaining homeostasis.
Compare and contrast the mechanisms of breathing and the exchange of gases.
Evaluate the processes of the digestive and cardiovascular systems and how they interface.
List the structure and functions of the organs of the urinary system and describe how they help to maintain homeostasis.
Outline the physiological processes of urine formation and urine elimination.
Define reproduction and explain its significance.
Compare and contrast the functions of the male and female sex hormones.
Identify histological slides of various cells and tissues in the body.

rows.title: Human Anatomy and Physiology II
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Identify gross anatomy of the Endocrine, Cardiovascular, Digestive, Respiratory, and Reproductive systems.
Explain the functions of the Endocrine, Cardiovascular, Digestive, Respiratory, and/or Reproductive systems.
Recognize the histological structures of the Endocrine, Cardiovascular, Digestive, Respiratory, and/or Reproductive systems.
Comprehend the overall physiological processes of the organ systems in the human body.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Name and list the different kinds of receptors of the somatic and special senses, and describe their sensations.
Explain how the eye functions and identify the parts of the eye from cornea to optic nerve.
Explain how the ear functions and identify the parts of the ear from the auricle to the vestibular and cochlear nerves.
Describe the structure and functions of the special connective tissue known as blood.
Compare and contrast the agranulocytes and granulocytes.
Explain how a differential white cell count can assist in diagnosis of pathology.
Discuss the components of plasma and the importance and relative concentrations of plasma proteins.
Explain how blood is an important transport media, a regulator of body temperature, and important in the defense of the body.
List all of the components of the cardiovascular system including the structure of the heart and its physiological functions, blood vessels, circulatory pathways, and blood pressure.
Trace the flow of blood through the heart.
Compare and contrast the systemic and pulmonary circulations.
Explain the complications of partial occulsion of the coronary arteries.
Trace the flow of food through the alimentary canal.
Discuss the steps of digestion, their sequence and relative importance.
Explain how the digestive system with chemicals caustic enough to digest any protein, does not digest itself in the process.
Explain and discuss nutrition and the metabolic processes which aid digestion and health.
Compare vitamins and minerals and their respective functions.
Explain and discuss the organs of the urinary system, both macroscopic and microscopic makeup.
Explain the physiological processes that filter the blood and form urine.
Illustrate how the kidney controls blood pressure and protects itself in the bargain.
Compare and contrast chemical buffers and physiological buffers.
Describe and identify all of the anatomical structures of the male reproductive system.
Discuss the physiology of the male reproductive system.
Describe and identify all of the anatomical structures of the female reproductive system.
Discuss the physiology of the female reproductive system.
Explain the role of the sex hormones in the formation and regulation of the sexual characteristics and reproduction cycles.
Discuss pregnancy, parturition, and infant development.
Explain possible complications and pathologies of pregnancy, parturition, and infant development.
Show how genetics affects an individual's anatomy and physiology, and discuss the advances in genetics that may remove some long standing problems and diseases.
Indicate important differences between hormonal and neural controls of body functioning.
List the major endocrine organs, describe their locations in the body, and discuss their respective hormones and hormone actions.
Describe the general location, histological structures, and functions of lymph nodes.
Describe the structure and distribution of lymphatic vessels, and note their important functions.
Compare and contrast the nonspecific and specific body immune defenses.
Explain the nonspecific cellular and chemical defenses of the immune system.
Compare and contrast the cell-mediated and humoral immune responses.
Identify the organs forming the respiratory passageway(s) in descending order until the alveoli are reached.
Describe the makeup of the respiratory membrane, and relate its structure to its function.
Exlain and compare the various lung volumes and capacities. Indicate the types of information that can be gained from pulmonary function tests.
Compare the causes and consequences of chronic bronchitis, emphysema, and lung cancer.

rows.title: Cultural Anthropology
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: Evaluate the conceptual frameworks that drive the practice of cultural anthropology in relation to the promotion of social justice.
Apply a relativist attitude in analyzing a social problem from various cultural perspectives.
objectives: Explain the role of cultural anthropology within the broader discipline of anthropology.
Analyze and reflect on the anthropological concept of culture in relation to key theoretical perspectives.
Demonstrate an understanding of anthropological concepts including ethnicity, gender, political organization, economic systems, kinship, rituals, and belief systems.
Apply and appraise a relativist view to the study of cultural difference.
Explain the main method of studying culture and interpret ethical implications of practicing such.
Evaluate the relation between globalization and culture.

rows.title: Native Peoples of North America
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Critical Thinking: Compare and contrast major events and themes in United States history from the perspectives of Native Americans.
Sources: Interpret primary and secondary sources and utilize them to draw conclusions about the Native American experience.
Historical Processes: Analyze broad patterns of change within and among various Native American cultures from pre-European contact to present.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:

Differentiate and appraise the various anthropological theories regarding the peopling of the New World. Compare and contrast the adaptations made by prehistoric Native Americans to differing ecological zones.
Differentiate among the various Native American cultures.
Discuss the different interactions of Native Americans with the French, Dutch, British, and Spanish and evaluate how those interactions initially impacted Native American cultures.
Examine the impact of European and American wars on relations with and between Native Americans.
Evaluate the roots and ramifications of the relationship between Native Americans and the U.S. Federal Government.

Critically review how struggle, resistance, racial and social justice, solidarity, and liberation, as experienced and enacted by Native Americans are relevant to current and structural issues such as communal, national, international, and transnational politics as, for example, in immigration, reparations, settler-colonialism, multiculturalism, language policies.

Analyze and articulate concepts of ethnic studies, including but not limited to race and ethnicity, racialization, equity, ethnocentrism, eurocentrism, white supremacy, self-determination, liberation, decolonization and anti-racism, as analyzed in Native American Studies.

Apply theory and knowledge produced by Native American communities to describe the critical events, histories, cultures, intellectual traditions, contributions, lived-experiences and social struggles of those communities with a particular emphasis on agency and group-affirmation.

rows.title: Language and Culture
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: Analyze the relation between language and culture through the lens of linguistic anthropology.
Apply a sociolinguistic perspective in evaluating the use of linguistic practices in intercultural contexts.
objectives: Explain anthropological approaches to the study of language, speech, and communication.
Consider the relationship between language and culture.
Identify the biological and cultural origins of and basis for language.
Analyze the structural properties of language.
Analyze a sampling of world languages, including nonverbal language, using methods of linguistic anthropology.
Discuss the relationship between language practices and social life and interpret the social consequences of language ideologies.
Evaluate ideas of language acquisition and language change.

rows.title: Introduction to Biological Anthropology - Honors
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: Analyze the processes and effects of key evolutionary mechanisms and genetic principles.
Explain the relation of modern humans to other primates, including hominins (or hominids) by applying knowledge of evolution and classification.
Honors: Apply knowledge of the STS (science and technology studies) perspective through creation and completion of an individualized research project.
objectives: Part 1 - Common Course Numbering Objectives:
Demonstrate an understanding of the scientific method and an ability to interpret data to arrive at reasoned conclusions.
Identify the principles of human inheritance, molecular biology, genetics, and evolutionary processes from the perspective of biological anthropology.
Identify the biological and cultural factors responsible for human variation.
Identify and compare primate and hominin species in terms of their osteological, morphological, and/or behavioral adaptations.
Part 2 - Local Course Objectives:
Describe the role of biological anthropology within the broader discipline of anthropology.
Apply and evaluate the scientific method.
Connect the ideas of key thinkers to one another in the context of the development of evolutionary theory.
Utilize and evaluate principles of Mendelian, molecular, and population genetics.
Interpret and measure the impact of forces of evolution on the genotypes and phenotypes of variable populations.
Compare the behavior and anatomy of living primates, including humans.
Describe and interpret phylogenies of ancestral and living primates, focusing on human evolution.
Summarize interpretations of the fossil record, including dating methods, as well as of the fossil evidence for human evolution.
Compare distinct groupings of hominids (or hominins).
Explain human variation in terms of both evolutionary theory and biocultural processes.

Honors: Consider the perspective of science and technology studies (STS) through interpretation of a primary source and applications of STS perspectives to reframe knowledge of a subject covered in the course.

rows.title: Biological Anthropology Lab - Honors
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Base Course: Course Student Learning Outcomes
Demonstrate understanding of the scientific method, genetics, and evolutionary processes to interpret human origins, adaptation, and variation.
Examine and compare primate and hominin anatomical, behavioral, fossil, and genetic evidence to evaluate evolutionary relationships and trends.
Investigate modern human diversity, explaining the interaction of biology and culture in shaping variation while recognizing the invalidity of race as a biological concept.
Demonstrate use of the scientific method to explore human and non-human evolution and human variation using the methods and techniques of biological anthropological research.
Demonstrate knowledge of human and non-human primate evolutionary history and the evolutionary significance of human variation.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Base Course: Course Objectives
Demonstrate an understanding of the scientific method and an ability to interpret data to arrive at reasoned conclusions.
Describe the principles of human inheritance, genetics, and evolutionary processes.
Identify and compare primate and hominin species in terms of their osteological,morphological, and/or behavioral adaptations.
Analyze a scientific argument, define its various elements, and evaluate its strengths and weaknesses.
Construct a model of DNA. Transcribe and translate a DNA code to construct a model protein.
Employ principles of Mendelian genetics to determine offspring genotype and phenotype probabilities.
Construct a cladogram based on primitive and derived traits.
Apply models of evolution to explain the process of change in specific case studies.
Identify and name the cranial and postcranial bones of the human skeleton.
Analyze the skeletal material of primates and determine the significance of morphological features and patterns.
Analyze the skeletal material of early hominin fossils. Compare and contrast features associated with bipedalism, cranial capacity, and tool use capability.
Analyze the skeletal material of fossils from the genus Homo. Compare and contrast features associated with cranial capacity and tool use capability.
Analyze the significance of genetic data from a variety of human populations.
Analyze human skeletal material to determine sex, age, and stature.
Formulate a hypothesis, develop a research design to test that hypothesis, conduct original research using one or more anthropological research methods and analyze data.
Conduct a review of literature, consulting scholarly journals as appropriate.
Write a report of their research in APA format, including an introduction, hypothesis, methods, results and discussion.
Submit an abstract of their research to an undergraduate or professional conference and if accepted, present the findings of their research.

rows.title: History of Modern Art
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Identify, discuss and critically analyze important and relevant works of art and architecture in Modern Art.
Critically evaluate the impact of art and architecture on the societies in which the artists and craftsman worked.
Understand art movements,newly developed modern art processes,and the inter-connected relationship of technologies and fine art.
Understand the impact of cultural, social, political, environmental issues, and more on the artists of the time and the resulting works that were created.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Identify and understand the basic visual vocabulary and art history terms.
Demonstrate the ability to compare and contrast representative works of art with the use of visual vocabulary and appropriate art historical terminology.
Analyze, discuss and differentiate the representative art works and architecture within socio-political, cultural and historic circumstances.
Compare, contrast and critique artwork in a historical as well as cultural context.
Analyze, discuss, interpret, and distinguish the role of the artists within movements in art and architecture covered in this course.

rows.title: Foundations of Two-Dimensional Design
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Apply the Principles and Elements of Two-Dimensional Design within design and fine art context.
Evaluate, analyze, disucss, and critique their own compositional works and the works of others.
Identify, evaluate, analyze, and employ the Elements and Principles of Two-Dimensional Design with other areas within the Visual Arts.
Critically discuss process, concepts and aesthetics within a two-dimensional work of art.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Discuss the elements and principles of two-dimensional design including line, color, texture, value, shape, scale/proportion, repetition, rhythm/unity, and emphasis.
Apply the elements and principles of design to work on a two-dimensional plane.

Analyze the technical and aesthetic potential of and employ a variety of traditional and non-traditional media in a series of projects that incorporate the elements and principles of two-dimensional design.
Translate personal and cultural ideas, perspectives and experiences into two-dimensional images using both formal and conceptual approaches.
Identify, analyze and employ the elements and principles of design with other areas within the field of visual art.
Discuss, analyze, evaluate and critique their own two-dimensional compositions and the compositions of others.

rows.title: Drawing I
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Students successfully learn basic skills strategies, and techniques of direct observational and freehand drawing.
Students successfully develop conceptual and compositional skills.
Students explore traditional, non-traditional contemporary techniques using a variety of media to engage in self-expression.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Demonstrate fundamental skills of observational and freehand drawing.
Discuss processes, concepts and aesthetics of drawing.
Critique and evaluate their own drawings and the drawings of others.
Develop skills and understanding in the importance of an excellent presentation of their work.
Develop an appreciation and understanding of the conceptual and practical basis of varied media, and the properties of each.
Practice safe handling of materials.

rows.title: Painting I
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Develop basic skills of painting.
Understand the fundamentals of color theory and composition as it pertains to painting.
Critique, evaluate and analyze basic painting techniques, strategies, and processes.
Create paintings with understanding of subject and content as a means of self expression.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Discuss color, color theory and composition as they apply to the field of painting.
Produce paintings that demonstrate an understanding of color and application of color theory and imagery.
Make visual and conceptual connections between the fundamental techniques of painting and the contemporary art world.
Discuss, analyze, evaluate and critique their own paintings and the paintings of others.

rows.title: Sculpture
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:

Demonstrate an understanding of sculptural techniques, development and understanding of form and form relationships within the physical world through working with traditional and non-traditional materials and techniques.
Develop an understanding of step by step process, from concept to to sculptural object.

Demonstrate learned knowledge of various genres of sculpture, of artists who work within those genres, and an understanding of the place that sculpture holds in art of the past and within the contemporary art world.
Understand, and skillfully use learned principles and elements of three-dimensional as it pertains to creating sculpture.
Learn to skillfully use various tools, processes, materials, and techniques.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Identify and understand the basic language of sculpture.
Demonstrate the use and care for the tools employed in making sculpture.
Demonstrate the ability to use a variety of materials employed in making sculpture, both traditional and non-traditional materials.
Identify, plan and create sculpture that incorporates reductive and additive techniques.
Apply learned skills of presentation and installation.
Learn critique skills to evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of their peers and their own sculpture.

rows.title: Life Drawing II
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Develop further fundamental life drawing skills that explores artistic concepts and styles.
Approach the study of life drawing through a more detailed and complex lens that informs the student's work.
Explore personal creative expression using various traditional and non-traditional media.
Explore through research, that which will inform the student's artistic experience and creative art work.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Render human figure to scale from observation of the model with greater accuracy and attention to anatomical details.
Make informed chocies regarding traditional and experimental drawing media and their applications.
Apply the principles and elements of design and fundamental skills of figure drawing to a series of more complex and sophisticated drawings.
Make visual and conceptual connections between intermediate-level figure drawing techniques and the contemporary art world.
Discuss, analyze, evaluate and critique their own drawings and the drawings of others.
Discuss and evaluate in greater depth the historical and contemporary trends in figure drawing in a global context.
Prepare and present a portfolio of work in multiple mediums and formats that demonstrates intermediate-level figure drawing techniques.

rows.title: Survey of Art from Prehistory to the Medieval Era -Honors
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Base Course: Course Student Learning Outcomes
Demonstrate awareness of artworks, styles and methods of production in the art of the Prehistoric era through Medieval.
Understand studied works as expressions of individual and human value within historical and social context.
Respond critically and analytically to works of art and architecture created in the Prehistoric through Medieval eras.
Better comprehend the physical and intellectual demands required of the artist.
Discuss and evaluate verbally, as well as in written form the works created in Prehistoric through Medieval eras.
Identify, discuss and analyze important and relevant works of art and architecture from Pre-History to Medieval Art.
Critically evaluate the impact of art and architecture on the societies in which the artists and craftsman worked.
Learn relevant and contemporary research practices to develop the ability to write about the arts and architecture of the time period of study.
Present research in an organized and thoughtful manner both orally and in written form.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Base Course: Course Objectives
Common Course Objectives
Identify, examine, and assess representative works of art and architecture from prehistory to the medieval era employing appropriate art historical terminology.
Analyze works of art and architecture in terms of aesthetic, socio-political, religious,historical, technological, and cultural contexts in which they were created.
Develop critical thinking, information literacy, and problem solving through an engagement with art, architecture, artists, and patrons from prehistory to the medieval era.
Additional Course Objectives
Articulate an understanding of and demonstrate an appreciation of the value and importance of art museums, galleries and other cultural institutions within their communities.
Honors Course Objectives
Critically evaluate artworks utilizing a methodology appropriate for the field in both written and oral form.

rows.title: Survey of Art from the Renaissance to Contemporary - Honors
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: When shown an image of a major work of art, the student will correctly identify the name, country or place of origin and date.
When asked to analyze the difference between two major works of art, the student will effectively compare and contrast styles and themes portrayed in the work.
objectives: Part 1 - Common Course Numbering Objectives:
Identify, examine, and assess representative works of art and architecture from the Renaissance to the contemporary period employing appropriate art historical terminology.
Analyze works of art and architecture and critique them in terms of aesthetic, socio-political, religious, historical, technological, and cultural contexts in which they were created.
Develop critical thinking, information literacy, and problem solving through an engagement with art, architecture, artists, and patrons from the Renaissance to the contemporary period.
Part 2 - Local Course Objectives:
Identify major works of art and architecture from the Renaissance through the 21st century and discuss their stylistic attributes with the larger context of the period in which they were created.
Define the various styles of art and demonstrate the ability to compare and contrast stylistic aspects and trends using correct art historical terminology.
Perform close visual analysis of images using formal and iconographic tools.
Critically analyze the concepts that define and distinguish Western art and demonstrate the ability to discuss these concepts contextually.

Evaluate works of art in relation to the sociological, religious, historical, and cultural context in which they were created and become acquainted with the many purposes for which visual arts are created and the multiple contexts in which they acquire meaning and value.
Honors: Compare and contrast Renaissance Art and the impact of Contemporary Art works to the 21st century.
Honors: Evaluate the impact of Indigenous creative gestures to Cubism, Dadaism, Surrealism, Assemblage, Modernism and Contemporary Art.
Honors: Research and evaluate the validity of performance art as an art form from a historical perspective.

rows.title: American Sign Language I - Honors
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:

Expressive Communication: Students will demonstrate signed ASL proficiency with proper production and clarity, speed and fluency, non-manual markers, and grammatical concepts, with an accuracy level of 70%+ (for a “3” score) or 85%+ (for a “4” score). Topics will include vocabulary covered in Signing Naturally units 1-5.

Receptive Communication and Linguistics: Students will interpret ASL segments containing vocabulary from units 1-5 with an accuracy level of 70%+ (for a “3” score) or 85%+ (for a “4” score) and demonstrate understanding of ASL grammar structures and concepts.

Cultural Diversity and Appreciation: Students will demonstrate appropriate knowledge of the Deaf Community regarding social interactions, beliefs, values, arts, literature, entertainment, diversity, and current events, at a superficial level. They will interact with, members of the Deaf Community, compare and contrast cultural norms, and appreciate the similarities and differences within the Deaf community and in comparison, with their own. Upon completion, students will reflect on their language use, strengths, areas for improvement, and outline a specific plan for continual language growth.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Introduce self and interact in Deaf culturally appropriate ways including getting a Deaf person’s attention, asking for repetition, and using a culturally appropriate style of communication

Engage in conversations about a variety of basic topics including introductions, personal information, academics, family and relationships, residences and communities, daily/weekly/monthly schedules, and leisure activities.

Use basic ASL grammar structure, including y/n-questions, wh-questions, rhetorical questions, topic/comment sentence structure, directional verbs, real world orientation and spatial agreement, contrastive structure, and simple classifiers.
Incorporate appropriate facial expressions and non-manual signals, pronouns, fingerspelling, loan signs, and cardinal and ordinal number structures into basic conversations.
Compare and contrast communication modes used by Deaf persons and the advantages and disadvantages of these modes.
Discuss in an informed manner the social, medical, and educational issues faced by Deaf persons in the United States.

rows.title: American Sign Language II-Honors
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:

Expressive Communication: Students will demonstrate signed ASL proficiency with proper production and clarity, speed and fluency, non-manual markers, and grammatical concepts, with an accuracy level of 70%+ (for a “3” score) or 85%+ (for a “4” score). Topics will include vocabulary covered in Signing Naturally units 7-11.

Receptive Communication and Linguistics: Students will interpret ASL segments containing vocabulary from Signing Naturally units 7-11 with an accuracy level of 70%+ (for a “3” score) or 85%+ (for a “4” score) and demonstrate understanding of ASL grammar structures and concepts.

Cultural Diversity and Appreciation: Students will demonstrate appropriate knowledge of the Deaf Community regarding social interactions, beliefs, values, arts, literature, entertainment, diversity, and current events, at a intermediate level. They will interact with members of the Deaf Community, compare and contrast cultural norms, and appreciate the similarities and differences within the Deaf community and in comparison, with their own. Upon completion, students will reflect on their language use, strengths, areas for improvement, and outline a specific plan for continual language growth. They will compare and contrast cultural norms between Hearing, Deaf, and deaf cultures (yes, Deaf and deaf are two different groups), and explain the values held by each group in terms of hearing status, language use, social circles, and political perspectives on deafness.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:

Introduce self and interact in Deaf culturally appropriate ways including getting a Deaf person’s attention, interrupting a conversation, opening and closing a conversation, providing feedback, and using a culturally appropriate style of communication
Engage in conversations about a variety of basic topics including food, personal appearances, housing and floor plans, finances and the workplace, wellness and fitness, and destinations

Use basic ASL grammar structure, including y/n-questions, wh-questions, rhetorical questions, topic/comment sentence structure, directional verbs, real world orientation and spatial agreement, contrastive structure, and simple classifiers

Incorporate appropriate facial expressions and non-manual signals, pronouns, fluent fingerspelling, loan signs, roleshifting, and various number structures such as cardinal/ordinal number, clock numbers, and money signs into conversations
Compare and contrast communication modes used by Deaf persons and the advantages and disadvantages of these modes
Discuss in an informed manner the social, medical, and educational issues faced by Deaf persons in the United States
Demonstrate an understanding of the differences between hearing and Deaf cultures, in regards to language, norms, and mores

rows.title: American Sign Language III-Honors
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Interpret visual/signed ASL at an intermediate level
Demonstrate language proficiency by signing American Sign Language at an intermediate level

Demonstrate advanced knowledge of the Deaf community regarding social interactions, beliefs, values, arts, literature, entertainment, and diversity/multiculturalism (various identities and intersectionality with different languages used in USA)
Define the concept of culture, appreciate other cultures and interact with members of those cultures in relation to their own
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Communicate comfortably, appropriately and effectively in conversations discussing language conventions, narratives, storytelling, history, and classifiers of various sorts.

Demonstrate comprehension and production of ASL grammatical strategies such as; role shifting, time indicators to specify tense, non-manual markers to indicate distance and location of items, use of both hands to indicate relation of items, inflection for temporal aspects such as recurring and continual, spatial agreement, plain verbs, transitions, narrative structures, sequencing orders, use of continuity, and descriptive and instrumental classifiers.

Compose and demonstrate ASL dialogues and/or narratives with ASL linguistic functions expressing a complaint, making a suggestion and requests, describes a life event, describes a weekend activity, tell a family immigration history, and describing items of various types and from various perspectives.

Apply sensitivity to Deaf culture in staged role-play interactions in terms of regulating the pace of a conversation in ASL, opening and resuming a conversation, and directing and maintaining attention.
Identify the differences in conversational patterns and linguistics of the Deaf and hearing communities.
Identify contemporary issues facing diverse members of the Deaf community within the United States.

Demonstrate a continued sensitivity of the Deaf and the needs within the community through attendance of Deaf events, and involvement in schools, institutions and organizations serving the Deaf persons.

rows.title: American Sign Language V
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Expressive Communication: Students will demonstrate language proficiency by signing American Sign Language at an intermediate to advanced level.
Receptive Communication: Students will interpret visual/signed ASL at an intermediate to advanced level.
Deaf Culture Appreciation: Students will define the concept of culture, appreciate other cultures and interact with members of those cultures in relation to their own
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Demonstrate ASL receptive and productive fluency at an intermediate/advanced level on a variety of topics.
Accurately recognize and interpret ASL idioms and colloquialisms as well as use them appropriately in expressive communication.
Identify idioms within the English language and accurately translate into ASL.
Incorporate advanced classifiers into everyday communication.
Compare ASL and English grammar structures and discuss similarities and differences.
Accurately translate concepts, stories, and articles from English into an imagistic form of ASL.

Analyze contemporary issues facing the Deaf community (including marginalized members and different language backgrounds) and effectively demonstrate public speaking skills by presenting information on current events within the Deaf community as well as research articles.
Create a bilingual (ASL and English text) or trilingual (ASL, English text and Spanish text) resume website for future employers.

rows.title: Introduction to Interpreting for the Deaf
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Define the duties and obligations of interpreters, as well as the Code of Ethics that governs their behavior.
Appropriately use interpreting terminology commonly used in the field.
Demonstrate correct conceptual and linguistic interpretation from ASL to English and English to ASL.
Adapt ASL register to match individual interpreting settings.
Identify diversity within the d/Deaf community and adapt communication to fit consumers’ needs.
Incorporate metacognitive strategies to conduct self-analysis of skills.
Analyze contemporary issues facing interpreters today.
Demonstrate a deeper sensitivity of the Deaf community and the need for professionals in the field.

rows.title: Essential Communication for Customer Service
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Engage in an introductory conversation: greet a client, introduce themselves and spell their name, ask the other person for their name, inquire about assistance needed.
Engage in basic conversation including information on Deaf status, identifying people, and discussing close relatives, while using personal, possessive, and plural pronouns when appropriate.
Ask questions and seek clarification when miscommunications occur.
Count from 1-100 with proper grammatical formatting.

Ask questions and seek clarification when miscommunications occur.
Count from 1-100 with proper grammatical formatting.

rows.title: Essential Deaf Culture for Effective Customer Service
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Explain the general concept of colonialism and why this framework resonates with the experiences of Deaf individuals.
Define the newly coined term, "Surdinalism," and understand its implications within the Deaf community.
Differentiate between the medical pedagogy and culturo-linguistic pedagogy in the context of Deaf culture.
Recall and apply appropriate terminology, moving away from medical pedagogy, to redefine Deaf experiences positively using culturally and linguistically appropriate terms.

rows.title: Introduction to Astronomy Lab
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: Align and calibrate a telescope, pointing it at several objects, including the Moon, planets, bright stars, faint stars, and diffuse objects (clusters, nebulae, and galaxies).
Identify and explain how electromagnetic radiation and astronomical instruments are used to reveal the properties of stars and planets.
Recognize elements of the scientific method and present observations and measurements using scientifically accurate reports, including data and error analysis.
objectives: Part 1 - Common Course Numbering Objectives:
Collect, analyze, and interpret astronomical data to draw and communicate valid scientific conclusions.
Part 2 - Local Course Objectives:
Critically evaluate basic scientific literature involving astronomical concepts.
Apply basic scientific principles to analyze new situations.
Identify, examine, and distinguish basic astronomical features in the sky.
Recognize and discriminate celestial coordinate systems.
Describe and relate how light spectra are produced, and how light conveys information about the universe.
Examine image formation by lenses.
Outline and explain the principles and operation of various astronomical instruments.
Analyze the motion of moons, planets, stars, and galaxies.
Compare planetary properties (comparative planetology).
Construct astronomical models and physical systems.
Observe, describe, and distinguish moons, planets, nebulae, stars, and galaxies.
Examine and use astronomical software for observations, simulations, and analysis.
Support, practice, and synthesize the above learning objectives through directed laboratory work.

rows.title: Cell and Molecular Biology
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Identify and discriminate the criteria used in the taxonomy of organisms, including the three domain system of classification (taxonomy) and binomial nomenclature.
Explain the hierarchy of biological organization from subatomic particles to the cell.
List and describe the emergent properties associated with life such as the relationship between structure and function and the differences between complex biological molecules and living cells.
State the principles of metabolism including entropy, enthalpy, and energy production and apply them in the laboratory to explore metabolic reactions in living organisms.
List and diagram the parts of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells and interpret their functions and distinguish between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells in the laboratory.
Identify the parts of the eukaryotic cell such as the nucleus, vacuoles, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, cell wall (in plant cells) and cell membrane.
Describe the structure and function of cellular membranes, including membrane lipids and proteins, transport across biological membranes, and concepts of osmotic pressure and tonicity.
Apply the concepts involving the structure and function of cellular membranes in the laboratory to examine their effects on living cells.
Explain the reactions that occur during photosynthesis and cellular respiration.
Explain and demonstrate how enzyme inhibitors can inhibit metabolic reactions.
Outline and explain the process of photosynthesis and discuss its significance to all forms of life on Earth.

Compare and contrast the complex characteristics of photosynthetic pigments such as the chlorophylls, carotenes and xanthophylls by identifying significant molecular characteristics and separating them into their components using chromatography techniques.
List and discuss the major events that occur during mitosis and meiosis.
Identify the stages of mitosis and meiosis in eukaryotic cells.
Analyze karyotypes and predict consequences of aneuploidy.
List and define the principles of Mendelian genetics.
Predict genetic ratios by the use of Punnett squares and use pedigree charts to analyze inheritance patterns.
Compare and contrast the major events and molecules that are involved in the synthesis of proteins and nucleic acids.
Compare and contrast the structure and genetics of bacteria, viruses, viroids and prions.
Evaluate the significance of recombinant DNA technology to society.
Describe basic techniques of biotechnology and how they are used to create genetically modified organisms.
Demonstrate safe and proper use of biological laboratory equipment including a compound light microscope, spectrophotometer, micropipettor and electrophoresis equipment.
Apply basic descriptive statistics to test expectations in experimental data results.
Generate hypotheses, propose tests of hypothesises, and analyze research procedures for sources of error and uncontrolled variables.

rows.title: Populations and Organisms
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Properly apply binomial nomenclature and principles of classification to organisms.
Outline and critically discuss the principles of Darwinian evolution and the evidence supporting evolutionary theory.
Compare and contrast the anatomical and physiological traits of the major kingdoms of life, and relate the unique features of major phyla to evolutionary history and the logic of adaption.
Analyze case studies of population changes, identifying the potential influence of factors that may be driving speciation, such as reproductive barriers, natural selection, and genetic drift.
Identify the roles that define an organism in an ecosystem and predict consequences to individuals and populations of altering interacting elements of the abiotic and biotic environment.
Make objective scientific observations of biological phenomenon, generate hypotheses, design and execute tests of hypotheses, analyze results, and critically discuss outcomes of experimentation.
Build skills using standard laboratory and field biology procedures and equipment.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:

Critically examine the evidence supporting biological evolution, including biogeography, comparative anatomy, comparative embryology, the fossil record, molecular homologies, and laboratory experimentation.
Outline the arguments supporting various theories explaining the origins of the first life on Earth.

Prepare a timeline of the history of life, identifying major evolutionary events such as appearance of prokaryotes, eukaryotes, multicellularity, and diversification of animals. Describe the developmental processes for each evolutionary leap.
Compare and contrast the structural, physiological and ecological attributes of archaea, bacteria, protista, fungi, plants, and animals.

Differentiate the major evolutionary adaptions in structure and function that define the plant phyla and animal phyla, identifying these traits in living or preserved specimens and explaining their adaptive significance.
List and provide examples to illustrate the major factors that influence macroevolution, including natural selection, genetic drift, mutation, and reproductive isolation mechanisms.
Explain the major concepts of population dynamics and the role of population size, migration rates, and other influences on potential Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
Apply appropriate biological terminology to the interactions among members of a community and the abiotic factors that affect community ecology dynamics.

Develop a hypothesis, design an experiment to test that hypothesis, and carry out and evaluate the results of that experiment using simple statistical tools and a critical analysis of sources of error and potential uncontrolled variables.

Write a scientific report in the formal style appropriate for publication in a scientific peer-reviewed journal, edited for spelling, punctuation, and grammar, and including the citation of at least 3 sources from scientific journals.

Utilize common laboratory tools and equipment, including standard laboratory glassware, thermometers, calipers, electronic balances, spectrophotometers, dissecting instruments, light microscopes, and stereomicroscopes, with an emphasis on asepsis, personnel and materials safety, and methods of assessing accuracy and precision.
Present orally in small and/or large group, providing course-relevant information that the student has researched and organized and supported with some type of visual aids.

rows.title: Introduction to Biology with Lab
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Apply the scientific method to explore biological questions, make observations, collect and analyze data, and draw evidence-based conclusions.
Describe the basic structure and function of cells and explain how energy and matter flow through living systems.
Explain the principles of evolution and how they help us understand both the unity and diversity of life on Earth.
Identify and compare major groups of organisms in terms of structure, function, ecological roles, and evolutionary relationships.
Evaluate biological information and issues presented in everyday media and public discussions to make informed personal and societal decisions.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Apply the scientific method, including recognizing the elements of experimental design,gathering and analyzing data, and interpreting results.
Demonstrate scientific literacy by evaluating social, ethical, and equity issues connected tobiological sciences
Describe how living things are made of smaller structures that work together to enable theorganism to survive.
Compare how living things depend on each other and the physical environment as they interactto obtain, change, and exchange matter and energy.
Explain how the diversity of living things is the result of evolution of organisms throughmechanisms such as heredity, random change, and natural selection.
Collaborate on laboratory investigations of the biological content using appropriate, safemethods and equipment.

rows.title: Introduction to Business
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Students will be able to demonstrate a significant understanding of the fundamental concepts of accounting, business law, economics, communication, and marketing.
Students will be able to produce clearly written, concise analyses, and deliver clear, well-organized, persuasive oral presentations.
Students will be able to use accounting information to make informed decisions about the internal operations of a company.
Students will be able to demonstrate an understanding of the role planning, organizing, leading and controlling plays in organizational success.
Students will be able to identify and apply ethical principles in management decision making.
Students will be able to describe what marketing entails and shows how the components are implemented.
Students will be able to analyze, interpret and present economic data.

Students will demonstrate their understanding of the role digital technologies play in the success of organizations and will demonstrate proficiency in the use of digital technologies by solving business problems using those technologies.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Students will be able to identify and describe the competitive environments and forces that affect the internal and external operations of companies doing business in the global market.
Students will be able to define and describe free-market capitalism and how it differs from other economic systems, as well as the role of key U.S. economic indicators.
Students will be able to explain entrepreneurship and what it takes to be an entrepreneur.

Students will be able to discuss the challenges managers face to set ethical standards and encourage corporate social responsibility, structure organizations, manage production and operations, and human resources.
Students will be able to describe the role of accounting and financial information and the challenges facing managers involved in the financial planning process.
Cite the various ways the U.S. government affects, restricts, and protects the business.

rows.title: Entrepreneurship and Small Business Management
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Explain the importance of small business and entrepreneurship in our society.
Distinguish between the terms small business and entrepreneurial opportunity.
Explain the basic characteristics of entrepreneurs and describe several different kinds of entrepreneurship.
Define integrity, and understand its importance to small businesses.
Describe external and internal analyses that can shape the identification and selection of venture opportunities.
Identify the components of a formal marketing plan.
Describe the purpose of financial forecasting.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Describe the characteristics of an entrepreneur.
Prepare or analyze a marketing plan.
Evaluate the sources of financing.
Define the customer and describe customer loyalty.
Compare and contrast product and pricing strategies.
Compare and constrast advertising, marketing and promotion for small firms.
Define and describe a distribution system.
Discuss social responsibilities and the small business.
Discuss ethics and the small business.
Define distinctive characteristics of small firm management.
Develop a process for hiring, training and developing employees.
Evaluate forms of compensation and incentives for the small business employee.
Create an inventory management and operations process.
Define accounting activities in small firms.
Analyze financial performance based on accounting documents.
Analyze the valuation of a firm.
Compare and contrast sole proprietorships, franchises, and partnerships.

rows.title: Human Relations in the Workplace
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
earn and apply effective interpersonal and group communication strategies within the context of the workplace.
demonstrate effective listening behaviors, including comprehensive, critical and active listening.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Discuss the historical development of the study of human relations and organizational behavior.
Compare and contrast various models of organizational structure and behavior.
Describe the effect of personality, values, beliefs, attitudes, perception, self-esteem and needs on behavior within business organizations.
Discuss the role physical and emotional health has on performance in the workplace and demonstrate behaviors associated with healthy living.
Discuss strategies used by organization to promote wellness in the workplace.
Discuss the effect stress has on individuals in the workplace and demonstrate effective techniques for managing stress.
Analyze their communication style and compare and contrast that style with the styles of others.
Identify the basic factors affecting communication within the workplace.
Demonstrate effective verbal and nonverbal skills in order to communicate more effectively in the workplace.
Differentiate between workgroups and teams.
Discuss the impact of individual roles, group dynamics and cohesiveness on the success of workgroups and teams within business organizations.
Demonstrate effective small group communication skills.
Compare and contrast various models of leadership within organizations.
Demonstrate effective leadership skills including motivation, employee development and managing change, climates and conflict in the workplace.
Demonstrate effective customer service skills.
Describe the influence of cultural diversity in the workforce.
Choose appropriate strategies to manage differences and capitalize on diversity within business organizations.
Describe the impact information technology has on human relations in the workplace.
Utilize information technology effectively, selecting and using tools appropriate to the task.
Analyze the effect employment law has on human behavior within organizations.
Demonstrate the ability to practice ethical decision making in the workplace.

rows.title: Business Law
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: Accurately utilize key business law terminology.
Evaluate and formulate legally sound and practical solutions to legal issues.
Identify the key elements of legal contracts.
objectives: Recognize some of the ethical/legal dilemmas faced by businesses, including their legal implications.
Apply correct legal terminology in the selected areas of law affecting business transactions.
Name, define and relate the key basic areas of business law, including principles of substantive and procedural law and third-party rights.
Compare the basic elements of the American legal system, the federal and state court systems, and the alternatives to litigation.
Differentiate between the basic business legal entities and the advantages and disadvantages of each.
Describe the basic elements of a contract, identify possible contract defenses, and propose contract remedies in hypothetical fact patterns.
Explain patents, copyrights, and trademarks.
Classify and explain the elements of crimes and torts relating to business issues.
Distinguish amongst the different types of employment relationships and demonstrate the ability to analyze the appropriateness to given situations.
Recognize some of the basic issues of international law facing a business operating internationally in the global economy.

rows.title: Principles and Practices in Early Childhood Education
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Compare and contrast historical and current early childhood education perspectives, theories, and program types and philosophies.
Describe the role of the early childhood educator, including ethical conduct and professional pathways.
Identify quality in early childhood programs related to environment, curriculum, and teaching strategies.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:

Interpret best and promising teaching and care practices as defined within the field of early care and education's history, range of delivery systems, programs types, and philosophies and ethical standards.
Develop one's teaching philosophy and professional goals using sound foundations in early childhood education (ECE)

Assess early childhood settings, curriculum, and teaching strategies utilizing indicators of quality early childhood practice that support all children including those with diverse characteristics and their families
Examine the value of play as a vehicle for developing skills, knowledge, dispositions, and strengthening relationships among young children.
Examine a variety of guidance and interaction strategies to increase children's social competence and promote a caring classroom community.
Analyze the relationship between observation, planning, implementation and assessment in developing effective teaching strategies in positive learning and development.

rows.title: Child, Family and Community
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Describe socialization of the child focusing on the interrelationship of family, school and community.
Describe strategies for collaboration with families to support children's development and learning that are respectful, reciprocal, and engaging.
Identify community resources to support children and their families.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Compare historical and current theoretical frameworks of socialization.
Examine research and developmental theories related to socialization.
Identify how the child develops within a system and is influenced by multiple factors of socialization including the educational, political, and socioeconomic impacts on children and families.
Compare and contrast diverse family characteristics and perspectives of children and families.
Evaluate the impact of one’s own experiences on their relationships with children, families, and the community.
Describe the legal requirements and ethical responsibilities of professionals working with all children and families.

Compare and contrast educational systems and practices, including strategies for family engagement and building partnerships between early learning settings, schools, and community organizations and agencies.
Describe contemporary social issues and their effects on families and children.
Identify community resources to support young children’s learning and development and to support families’ needs.
Describe and analyze effective strategies that empower families and encourage family involvement in children's development.
Identify the need for and ways to participate in advocacy activities on behalf of young children and their families.

rows.title: Creative Science and Math Activities for Children
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: Create age appropriate activities for a preschool science and math program.
Analyze basic science and math concepts for young children.
Formulate goals and objectives for a preschool science and math program.
objectives: Analyze basic science and math concepts and determine which are developmentally appropriate for children birth through age eight.
Create a developmentally appropriate science and math environment for preschool classrooms.
Identify the scientific process skills: observing, comparing, measuring, classifying and predicting.
Identify the basic math concepts: classifying, ordering, seriation, patterning, number sense and counting.
Design activity lesson plans that examine fundamental science concepts in life science, physical science and earth science.
Design activity lesson plans that implement fundamental math concepts: classifying, simple reasoning, ordering, seriation, patterning, number sense and counting.

rows.title: Play and Materials for Children
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: Create age-appropriate play materials.
Explain age appropriate stages of play and developmental abilities of children.
Describe safe, interactive, aesthetic, and age appropriate indoor and outdoor physical play environments for young children.
objectives: Articulate the relationship between pedagogy, curriculum, play and inquiry-based learning as it relates to children's diverse interests and learning styles.
Identify theories, stages and development of play and developmental abilities of children.
Plan and implement a developmentally appropriate play experience with children.
Describe a developmentally appropriate pedagogy about facilitating children's play.
Design a physical play environment (inside and outside) for children.
Justify how resources foster the development of play and inquiry-based learning curriculum areas and can be used for assessment.
Create a play resource kit and explain how it relates to current pedagogy.
Identify the teacher's role in facilitating development in play and inquiry-based learning environments.
Apply professional ethics in data collection and reporting.

rows.title: Infant/Toddler Growth and Development
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Identify stages of infant and toddler development
Incorporate theory and research into assessment of development.
Establish and maintain a safe, healthy and high quality learning environment for infants and toddlers
Facilitate physical and cognitive competence, including language in infants and toddlers
Support social and emotional development
Identify services and support for infants and toddlers with special needs
Identify the components in establishing positive and productive relationships with families
Write and develop a philosophy for working with infants and toddlers based on developmentally appropriate practice

rows.title: Child Development Practicum
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Apply a variety of effective approaches, strategies and techniques for teaching in an early childhood classroom.
Design, implement and evaluate curriculum and environments based on observation and assessment of young children.
Analyze personal teaching experiences to guide and inform practice.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Apply a variety of effective approaches, strategies and techniques supporting positive and effective relationships with children and families.
Participate in the design, implementation and evaluation of curriculum activities that are based on observation and assessment of young children.
Integrate concepts regarding children's development and needs into planning and maintaining healthy, safe, respectful, supportive and challenging learning environments for all children.
Assume teaching and non-teaching responsibilities and demonstrate developmentally appropriate practices in an early childhood classroom
Incorporate current research and understanding of developmental theories into the selection of learning materials and experiences for young children.
Present and evaluate a variety of developmentally, culturally and linguistically appropriate play-based learning experiences.
Analyze classroom space and daily routines in terms of their effect on the behavior and interactions of children and teachers.
Integrate content areas and opportunities for development across the curriculum.
Model and facilitate appropriate problem solving, conflict resolution strategies, and social behaviors.
Analyze student teaching experiences to inform and guide future teaching practices.
Utilize an appropriate recordkeeping system to document, assess and track children's progress.
Demonstrate professional and ethical behavior.
Use professional written and verbal communication skills.
Critically assess one's own teaching experiences to guide and inform practice.

rows.title: Observation and Assessment in Early Childhood Education
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Evaluate the characteristics, strengths, limitations, and applications of contemporary observation and assessment tools for early childhood environments
Complete systematic observations and assessments in an early childhood environment using a variety of data collection methods to inform environment design, interactions, and curriculum.
Discuss the role of partnerships with other professionals and families in interpreting observational and assessment data.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Identify and compare the purpose, value and use of formal and informal observation and assessment strategies
Describe and evaluate the major characteristics, strength and limitations of selected assessment tools
Complete systematic observations, using a variety of methods of data collection to assess the impact of the environment, interactions with curriculum on children's development and behavior
Identify the role of partnership with families and other professionals in utilizing interpretations of observational data to inform teaching practices
Identify and evaluate logistical challenges, biases and preconceptions about assessing children
Observe, document, assess and interpret children's development in a variety of developmental domains
Identify the role of observation and assessment in intervention
Use the observation, documentation, and implementation cycle to suggest changes in curriculum for children and communicate changes with parents and colleagues

rows.title: Guidance of Young Children
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
To identify influences on children's behavior and appropriate guidance techniques based on the developmental level of the child and desired outcomes.
Demonstrate understanding of the influence of direct and indirect guidance strategies on children's behavior.
Describe the influence of personal beliefs, behavioral styles and child development knowledge on one's personal approach to guidance and interactions with young children
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Analyze children's behavior in view of developmental issues, family and cultural dynamics.
Compare and contrast theories of guidance.
Analyze and describe how to use guidance and discipline practices related to the developmental "ages and stages" of children.
Analyze and critique discipline trends
Identify types of child misbehaviors and propose appropriate interventions
Analyze personal experiences and how it impacts his/her guidance of children.
Examine guidance strategies for children with disabilities.
Propose and appraise skills necessary to positively address challenging behavior in young children.

rows.title: Administration I: Programs in Early Childhood Education
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: Apply administration skills related to various types of early care and education programs.
Apply knowledge of strategic and fiscal planning.
Evaluate the components of quality programs, facilities and operations.
objectives: Compare and contrast various program structures, philosophies and curriculum models.
Identify strategies to ensure equity and respect for children, families, staff and colleagues.
Summarize systems and methods to support sound fiscal operations in a variety of Early Childhood Education settings.
Demonstrate knowledge of regulations and compliance with regulatory systems.
Assess various methods and tools of evaluation.
Develop a site development plan for a center-based program that incorporates licensing regulations for both indoor and outdoor environments.
Develop an orientation process for new employees.
Examine the components of a safe and healthy environment for children.
Customize marketing materials to reflect the size and type of child care services needed in the community.
Customize curriculum content and teaching strategies to reflect program philosophy.
Examine effective policies and procedures for staffing and scheduling.

rows.title: Elementary Laboratory
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes

Demonstrate knowledge of the assessment, planning, implementation and documentation cycle in education.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Demonstrate the adult's role in socialization and development of the school age child through appropriate interactions in a public elementary school setting.
Identify basic stages of child growth and development as they apply to the school age child including: Physical, psychosocial, intellectual and moral development
Research and reflect on issues facing today's children
Demonstrate appropriate and effective child guidance techniques while working with school age children at an introductory level with direct supervision in a public elementary school setting
Observe and critique a school age environment to include use of inside and outside space
Recognize and describe individual differences among students, identifying strategies and adaptations used to address these differences

Demonstrate professionalism and the ability to utilize appropriate and effective communications in child, staff and parent relationships at an introductory level with direct supervision in a public elementary school setting
Identify the components of quality interactions in the relationships between child, family, school and the community
Demonstrate skill in understanding and implementing protocols for visiting schools and classrooms
Record and reflect on personal experiences involving interactions with school age children in an elementary school setting

rows.title: Child Growth and Development - Honors
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:

Identify the typical progression of development across all domains.
Describe the impact of multiple factors on development and well-being, including those related to biology, environment, culture, and social interactions.
Summarize major theories of child development.
Describe development of children from conception through adolescence in the physical, cognitive, language, social and emotional domains.
Identify cultural, economic and historical contexts that impact children's development.
Apply knowledge of development and major theoretical frameworks to developmental observations.
Analyze a topic in Child Development using research and APA style.

Differentiate characteristics of typical and atypical development.
Describe major developmental milestones for children from conception through adolescence in the areas of physical, cognitive, language, social, and emotional development.
Identify and analyze how biology as well as social, economic, historical and cultural contexts affect children's development.
Identify and compare major theoretical frameworks related to the study of human development.
Utilize research methodologies for and apply developmental theory to child observations.
Differentiate characteristics of typical and atypical development.
Identify and describe biological and environmental factors that influence children development across all domains, from conception to adolescence.
Research and analyze an approved child development topic based on a minimum of five empirical sources.
Formulate and express arguments in written and oral forms as related to an approved topic in child development.
Apply developmental theory to personal, real life experiences.

rows.title: Introduction to Organic Chemistry
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
