rows.title: Principles of Microeconomics
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of how equilibrium prime is determined by market forces using supply and demand diagrams. Show how changes in market forces can be expressed as a shift in either the supply or demand curve. Target a specific market (for example: gasoline, coffee, or airline tickets). Consider likely events that will change the market equilibrium. For each case draw a graph and show whether demand or supply will shift. Show also the effect on the equilibrium price and quantity.

Given information about the demand schedule of a Monopolistic firm and a simple cost structure, student will draw a graph showing demand, marginal revenue, and marginal cost. Students will show the monopoly profit-maximizing output and price in the graph. Then, a brief explanation of why monopolists do not produce a socially desired level of output should be made by reference to the graph.

List two distinct markets that exist on their college campus (groups of workers that are not easily substituted for one another). Identify the characteristic (such as a specific skill) that makes each labor market unique. Students will formulate the Marginal Revenue Product of Labor theory to suggest two good reasons for pay differences of the labor groups (occupations) they cite.
objectives: Part 1 - Common Course Number Objectives
Perform and interpret microeconomic calculations.
Apply microeconomic models to analyze market outcomes, including market failures and government policies.
Model how consumers and firms make decisions under a variety of market structures
Part 2 - Local Course Objectives

Identify and demonstrate knowledge of the nature and scope of economics, including the definition of "scarcity" and its consequences, with special emphasis on the importance of marginal analysis for economic problem-solving.
Analyze various supply and demand situations, illustrating the effects on the equilibrium price, and quantity of a given shift in supply and/or demand.
Identify and apply the necessary elements of a market system and compare them to other economic systems in a theoretical framework of the comparative economic systems perspective.
Apply the concept of price elasticity of demand and supply and discuss the determinants of each, including cross-price and income elasticities.

Interpret and develop economic graphs which emphasize equi-marginal analysis in preparation for analysis of consumer choice (utility-maximization) and cost minimization by utilizing indifference curves and isoquants.
Explain the law of diminishing marginal utility and how it relates to the law of demand, using real-world examples.

Analyze short-run and long-run cost curves, implicit and explicit costs, and economies/diseconomies of scale, including the derivation of total, average,average-variable, average-fixed and marginal cost curves to aid in explaining the theory of the firm.
Conduct a comparative study of the characteristics of the four major market structures (perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, and monopoly).
Use game theory concepts to analyze and evaluate asymmetric markets, moral hazard and adverse selection in specific market environments such as health care, insurance and financial markets.

Identify socially efficient allocations and evaluate the role of government (public choice) in dealing with market failures in distribution of factor income, positive and negative externalities, asymmetric information, and antitrust.
Elucidate the principles that explain international trade, including comparative advantage, terms of trade, and the impact of trade restrictions.
Compare the various exchange rate systems and explain specifically how exchange rates are determined under each system.

Analyze the role of the Federal Reserve Bank in combating inflationary and recessionary conditions in the economy. Discuss the use the three tools of monetary policy (reserve requirement, discount rate and open market operations), in this context.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:

Comprehend and interpret Earth-Sun relations and resulting seasonal changes.
Assess the formation of major landforms.
Analyze the distribution and classification of world climates and Earth’s biomes.
Consider the uneven impact of environmental pollution and climate change on socioeconomically disadvantaged communities, including communities of color and recent-immigrant communities.
objectives: Categorize the systems of atmosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere, and lithosphere and how they interact across Earth's surface.

Diagram the grid system of latitude and longitude, in terms of absolute global location, and apply knowledge of latitude to Earth-Sun relations and temperature patterns, and apply knowledge of longitude to global time and time zones.
Examine the scientific method within the context of selected geographic and environmental phenomena.

Analyze the ability of the tools of the geographer, including maps, globes, remote sensing devices, Google Earth, Geographic Information Systems (GIS), and Global Positioning Systems (GPS), to reveal spatial unevenness of human-environment interactions and overall environmental health.
Diagram the unequal distribution of thermal energy on Earth and relate it to global regions of wind and atmospheric pressure.
Analyze the interrelationship between latitude and solar energy (insolation) received at Earth's surface.
Inventory the world's wind, ocean current, and hydrologic patterns.

Assess the interrelationship between humans and the natural environment based upon cultural perceptions of and reactions to natural hazards and natural and anthropogenic causes of global climate change.

Evaluate relationships between human actions and environmental issues, and examine the impacts of environmental issues on human populations within the context of environmental racism and environmental justice.
Discuss the spatial correlation between environmental quality and socioeconomically disadvantaged communities, including communities of color.
Describe the world's general geographic pattern of vegetation, soil, and climate, comparing, for example, biome and climate regions.
Describe the basic geographic patterns of tectonic and volcanic activity.
Categorize gradational processes and resulting landforms.

Examine large-scale physical geographic features within California, including coastlines and beaches, mountains and valleys, deserts and forests, and caves and glacial artifacts, and explain their origins.

rows.title: Physical Geography Laboratory
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: Analyze and interpret mapping elements such as latitude, longitude, map scale, map projection, and topography.
Examine elements of weather and climate such as latitude, season, elevation, coastal versus continental location, orographic effect, wind patterns and air masses, and ocean currents.
Categorize igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks within the context of the rock cycle.
Identify landform shaping processes such as Plate Tectonics, volcanism, weathering, mass wasting, and erosion.
Consider the uneven impact of environmental pollution and climate change on socioeconomically disadvantaged communities, including communities of color and recent-immigrant communities.
objectives: Select the appropriate geographic tool or method, including maps, globes, Geographic Information Systems (GIS), Global Positioning Systems (GPS), and remote sensing, to address a variety of geographic problems, including the spatial unevenness of human-environment interaction and overall environmental health.
Categorize and interpret different types of maps, including thematic, reference, and topographic.
Diagram the Earth's grid system of latitude and longitude on a globe and map.
Locate cities and physical features, given latitude and longitude coordinates.
Calculate latitude and longitude coordinates for a given city or physical feature.
Employ atlases, globes, ArcGIS Online, Google Earth, and other geographic tools to appropriately locate cities and physical features.
Construct a climograph for a particular location by collecting weather data, including monthly average temperature and precipitation.
Evaluate climate regions, given climatic data for specific locations.

Assess the interrelationship between humans and the natural environment based upon cultural perceptions of and reactions to natural hazards and natural and anthropogenic causes of global climate change.

Evaluate relationships between human actions and environmental issues, and examine the impacts of environmental issues on human populations within the context of environmental racism and environmental justice.
Discuss the spatial correlation between environmental quality and socioeconomically disadvantaged communities, including communities of color.
Assess the geologic origin and history of representative rock specimens.
Produce a tectonic map, given seismic, geologic age, and volcanic data.
Analyze selected topographic maps for specific karst, glacial, and fluvial geomorphic features.
Analyze selected topographic maps for slope and aspect, scale and distance measurement, and public land survey system.
Synthesize textbook and field observations, including atmospheric, biologic, hydrologic, and geologic elements, into a coherent field report.

Experiment successfully with a variety of basic geography laboratory equipment, including maps, globes, rulers, calculators, colored pencils, compasses, sling psychrometers, global positioning system devices, and cameras.
Categorize solstice and equinox data for selected locations (latitudes) and discuss how western and non-western societies have understood and adapted to seasonal changes.
Apply the scientific method to in- and out-of-class laboratory exercises.

rows.title: Investigations in Weather and Climate
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:

Identify how the Earth’s oceans and atmosphere are responsible for the distribution of the energy received from the sun through an analysis of the interaction of global atmospheric and ocean circulation patterns.

Identify and understand that the climate at different places on Earth is dependant upon the amount and duration energy received at that location, and that the climate dictates the type of vegetation as well as the weather conditions.
Utilize critical thinking skills to interpret, apply and/or evaluate the concept of scale (spatial and time) as it pertains to the geosciences.
Collect, analyze and interpret information and clearly articulate the results through their writing, speech or other acceptable style of presentation.
Analyze and interpret meteorological data sets and develop a weather forecast over several days.
Analyze climate data from a particular location and determine the type of climate of that locale.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Describe and elaborate on the energy balance of the Earth-atmosphere system.
Desribe the conditions and forces that create atmospheric motion and the pressure patterns, wind systems and global circulation patterns that result.
Describe and discuss the moisture conditions that can exist in the atmsophere, and the precipitation processes that can result.
Describe how and where clouds form in the atmosphere.
Describe and explain the types of weather systems.
Describe and analyze the weather conditions responsible for the formation of extreme events that occur in the atmosphere.
Identify, classify and describe the atmospheric data utilized on weather maps, radar imagery and satellite technology.
Identify and describe global climate distribution, and recognize the relationship between climate, biogeography and soils.
Identify and analyze the causes and implications of global climate change.

rows.title: World Regional Geography
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Distinguish between formal culture regions and functional culture regions recognizing the concepts of culture boundaries, core areas and codes.
Compare and contrast the political, social and economic traits that characterize developed and technologically less developed regions of the world.
Outline the impact of humankind on the rainforests of the world, indicating the long term implications.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Make a distinction between formal culture regions and functional culture regions recognizing the concepts of culture boundaries, core areas and codes.
List key culture traits that make the landscapes of each of the major culture regions of the world distinctive.
Recognize the significant landforms of each of the major culture regions of the world.
Describe the broad climatic patterns that characterize the culture regions of the world.
Compare and contrast the political, social and economic traits that characterize developed and technologically less developed regions of the world.
Describe ways that humankind has developed to deal with the arid lands of the world.
Outline the impact of humankind on the rainforests of the world, indicating the long term implications.
Compare and contrast market and command economic systems as they relate to the major culture regions of the world.
Compare and contrast the basic elements of urbanism First and Third World countries of the world.

rows.title: Introduction to Geographic Information Systems
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Define Geographic Information Systems (GIS).
Identify and evaluate GIS data sources and the importance of metadata.
Demonstrate the process of converting analogue data to digital data for use in a GIS.
Identify, compare and contrast vector and raster GIS.
Evaluate the capabilities of various GIS software programs.
Apply cartographic principles of scale, resolution, projection and data management to a problem of a geographic nature.
Apply spatial analysis functions on a GIS to solve a Geospatial problem.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Display qualitative and quantitative data in graphical format using ArcGIS software

Perform basic GIS (Geographic Information Systems) queries to include buffering, joining and selection

Discover, hypothesize, text, and display findings using ArcGIS

outcomes: Review the major geologic processes that have been involved in the formation of California's varied landscape.
Identify the boundaries of California's twelve geomorphic (physiographic) provinces.
Describe the principal geologic features of each of the twelve geomorphic (physiographic) provinces.
Summarize the geologic history of each of the twelve provinces, including the geologic ages of the major rock units and outstanding geologic structures.
objectives: Describe the major geologic structural features of California.

Evaluate the dominant geologic processes affecting each geomorphic province.

Examine the significance of the San Andreas Fault system as a plate boundary in respect to California's geologic development.

Inspect the boundaries of the major geomorphic provinces in California on topographic maps and aerial photographs.
Analyze evidence on geologic maps and cross-sections to describe the sequence of geologic evolution that led to the observable features.
Assess the geologic hazards and risks associated with different geomorphic (physiographic) provinces of California.

rows.title: Elements of Oceanography

rows.lead: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: Apply the scientific method to assess Earth systems and components (e.g. atmosphere, biosphere, hydrosphere, geosphere, etc.).
Analyze large-scale atmospheric and oceanic circulation patterns.
Consider the temporal nature of ocean ecosystems and the interconnected nature of ocean life.
Interpret the formation and evolution of ocean basins.

Explain the disproportionate impacts of sea level rise, coastal flooding, coastal pollution, coastal erosion, and overfishing on coastal and island communities of color, coastal aboriginal communities, and socioeconomically disadvantaged communities.
objectives: Diagram the general internal structure of the earth.

Analyze the marine conditions controlling the distribution of life in the oceans.

Categorize taxonomic hierarchy and understand the value of scientific nomenclature.
Assess the physical parameters that limit biological expansion into other marine life zones.
Examine world oceans using a variety of geospatial technologies, including Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and remote sensing.

Assess the causes and effects of significant environmental issues occurring throughout the world's oceans, including eutrophication, plastic pollutants, oil spills, coral bleaching, overfishing, ocean acidification, sea level rise, sea surface temperature increase, invasive species, increased container ship traffic, estuary habitat loss, and increased coastal development and urbanization.

Examine environmental justice issues related to the world's oceans, including illegal fishing, seafood slavery, folk traditions related to fishing, climate refugees, underrepresented voices, and disproportionate impacts upon socioeconomically disenfranchised coastal communities, coastal communities of color, and aboriginal coastal communities.
Value and recognize contributions of traditionally underrepresented scientists and voices to oceanographic research and solutions to oceanographic environmental issues.

Critique governing institutions and political processes within the United States and California.
Employ introductory political science research methods to contextualize contemporary political issues and operations in the United States and California.
Assess civil liberties and civil rights of individuals and groups as articulated in the U.S. and California Constitutions and subsequent court decisions.
Investigate the role of identity and political ideology in shaping public opinion and public policy in the United States and California.
Analyze how to effectively participate in politics at the national, state, county, and/or city levels.

rows.title: Theories of Personality
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Identify the major figures, schools, and terminology of the development of personality theory.
Discuss the historical context of specific approaches to personality.
Apply different theories of personality to specific fields of psychology: clinical, industrial, consumer, forensic, education, research.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Explain issues involving the definition of personality
Describe some theoretical models which have been used in the study of personality (e.g., structural, topographical, dynamic, developmental, functional, trait)
Identify the theories and historical contexts of individuals who engaged in pre-scientific speculation about personality (e.g., Plato, Hippocrates)
Explain why such theories are not scientific
Identify and define the key terms of psychoanalysis
Discuss the historical context of Freud's life and career
Discuss to what extent classical psychoanalysis can be viewed as a branch of science or as a cult
Apply psychoanalytic theory to discourse on clinical and social topics (e.g., women, religion, homosexuality)
Identify and define the key terms of Adler's theory
Discuss the scientific status of Adler's theory
Compare and contrast Adler's and Freud's theories, noting differences and similarities
discuss Adler's place in the development of psychological theory, who influenced him, and who was influenced by him
Apply Adler's theory to discourse on clinical and social topics
Identify and define the key terms of Jung's theory
Discuss the scientific status of Jung's theory
Compare and contrast Jung's and Freud's theories, noting differences and similarities
Discuss Jung's place in the development of psychological theory, who influenced him, and who was influenced by him
Apply Jung's theory to discourse on clinical and social topics

Identify the key terms and persons in the Neo-psychoanalytic and Dynamic Psychology movements (e.g., Rank, Erikson, Ego Psychology, Horney, Brown, Lacan, Ricoeur, Object Relations), discuss their place in the development of psychological theory, and apply them to discourse on clinical and social topics

Identify the key terms and persons in the Marxian psychology movement (e.g., Fromm, Marcuse, Reich), discuss their place in the development of psychological theory, and apply them to discourse on clinical and social topics

Identify the key terms and persons in the interpersonal psychology movements (e.g., Adler, Erikson, James, Mead, Vygotsky, Sullivan), discuss their place in the development of psychological theory, and apply them to discourse on clinical and social topics

Identify the key terms and persons in the Learning Theory (e.g., Pavlov, Watson, Skinner, Bandura), discuss their place in the development of psychological theory, and apply them to discourse on clinical and social topics

identify the key terms and persons in the Holistic and Humanistic movements (e.g., Adler, Jung, Lecky, Goldstein, Angyal, Allport, Maslow, Murray, Lewin, Rogers, Perls), discuss their place in the development of psychological theory, and apply them to discourse on clinical and social topics

Identify the key terms and persons in the trait movement (e.g., Hippocrates, Allport, Cattell, Eysenck, NEO-5, MMPI, Adorno, Bem, Friedman, Holland), discuss their place in the development of psychological theory, and apply them to discourse on clinical and social topics

Identify the key terms and persons in the cognitive psychology movement (e.g., Adler, Kelly, Ellis, Beck, Rotter), discuss their place in the development of psychological theory, and apply them to discourse on clinical and social topics

Identify the key terms and persons in the alternative psychology movements (e.g., Asian, Afro-centric, Mestizo, Womanist, Islamic, Christian, ecological), discuss their place in the development of psychological theory, and apply them to discourse on clinical and social topics
Discuss the key concepts of Positive Psychology (e.g., Dweck, Duckworth, Lyubormirsky, Seligman, Csikszentmihalyi): mindset, GRIT, flourishing, flow.

rows.title: Developmental Psychology: Lifespan
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Describe the sequences of physical, social, and cognitive changes associated with conception through aging, using the constructs and conceptual framework provided by psychological perspectives.
Discuss and predict age and gender differences and similarities throughout the lifespan
Identify, describe and critically evaluate the techniques and methods used by developmental psychologists
Identify, describe and critically evaluate classic and contemporary theory and research in the study of human growth and development.
Use library and electronic resources to locate current research related to specific topics in developmental psychology.
Critically analyze the knowledge acquired about human growth and development, and apply the insights gained to an understanding of one’s own growth and development.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Describe the sequences of physical, social, and cognitive changes associated with conception through aging, using the constructs and conceptual framework provided by psychological perspectives.
Identify, describe, and critically evaluate the techniques and methods used by developmental psychologists.
Identify, describe, and critically evaluate classic and contemporary theory and research in the study of human growth and development.
Identify and describe the contemporary issues and concerns within developmental psychology.
Use library resources to locate current research related to specific topics in developmental psychology.
Assess our culture’s view of childhood, adolescence, adulthood, and aging from an analysis of cross-cultural studies.
Analyze real-life situations involving infants, children, adolescents and adults in light of relevant theory and research in developmental psychology.
Critically analyze the knowledge acquired about human growth and development and apply this information to an understanding of the students' own growth and development.
Analyze elements of a scientific approach to understanding human development in a biopsychosocial context.
Identify possible causes or sources of developmental change and reasons for disturbances in the developmental process.

rows.title: Statistics for the Social and Behavioral Sciences
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:

Perform calculations on quantitative data commonly encounted in social science research in order to arrive at appropriate descriptive and inferential statistics (e.g., percent, mean, standard deviation, percentile, confidence interval, effect size, Pearson coefficient, chi squared, t-test, Analysis of Variance).
Interpret and construct tables (e.g., correlation matrix), graphs (e.g., frequency, scatterplot), and charts (e.g., pie, bar) that summarize data.
Select the appropriate descriptive and inferential statistics to employ when given scale(s) of measurement, research design, and normality of the distribution of a data set.
Explain the process of null hypothesis significance testing, confidence intervals, and effect size, and apply these to data sets.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Distinguish among different scales of measurement and their implications
Interpret data displayed in tables and graphically
Apply concepts of sample space and probability
Calculate measures of central tendency and variation for a given data set
Identify the standard methods of obtaining data and identify the advantages and disadvantages of each
Calculate the mean and variance of a discrete distribution
Calculate probabilities using normal and student's t-distributions
Distinguish the difference between sample and population distributions and analyze the role played by the Central Limit Theorem
Construct and interpret confidence intervals
Determine and interpret levels of statistical significance including p-values
Interpret the output of a technology-based statistical analysis
Identify the basic concept of hypothesis testing including Type I and II errors
Formulate hypothesis tests involving samples from one and two populations
Select the appropriate technique for testing a hypothesis and interpret the result
Use linear regression and ANOVA analysis for estimation and inference, and interpret the associated statistics

Use appropriate statistical techniques to analyze and interpret applications based on data from disciplines including business, social sciences, psychology, life science, health science, and education

rows.title: Introduction to Psychology
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: Identify, compare, and critically evaluate theory and research based ideas in a variety of psychology subfields and show the ability to apply these ideas to their lives, as assessed by a written assignment.
Analyze the consequences of different personal behavioral choices by applying psychological theory and research to their lives, as assessed by a written assignment.
objectives: Part 1 - Common Course Numbering Objectives:
Demonstrate fundamental knowledge and comprehension of major concepts, theoretical perspectives, historical and cultural contexts, and empirical findings within the broad discipline of psychology.

Use a scientific approach (including critical and creative thinking) to understand individuals’ mind and behavior within psychological, biological, sociocultural, and ethnocultural contexts while recognizing that biases filter experiences.
Apply psychological theories, concepts, and values to individual, interpersonal, group, and societal issues to demonstrate awareness of self and others.

Draw logical and objective conclusions about the mind and behavior from evidence to show how psychology evaluates, modifies, and supports its claims and counters unsubstantiated statements, opinions or beliefs.
Part 2 - Local Course Objectives:
Identify and critically evaluate major concepts, theoretical perspectives, research methods, core empirical findings, and historic trends in psychology.

Explain (including advantages and disadvantages), compare and synthesize ideas within major theoretical perspectives of psychology (e.g., behavioral, biological, cognitive, evolutionary, humanistic, psychodynamic, and socio-cultural).
Understand and apply psychological principles to the student's personal experience and social and organizational settings.

Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the following nine general domains: (1) biological bases of behavior and mental processes, (2) sensation and perception, (3) learning and memory, (4) cognition and consciousness, (5) individual differences, psychometrics, and personality, (6) social processes (including those related to socio-cultural and international dimensions), (7) developmental changes in behavior and mental processes that occur across the lifespan, (8) psychological disorders, and (9)emotion and motivation.
Describe and demonstrate an understanding of applied areas of psychology (e.g., clinical, counseling, forensic, community, organizational, school, health).
Distinguish between scientific and non-scientific methods of understanding and analysis as well as understand major ethical issues involved in psychological research methods.
Demonstrate critical thinking skills and information competence as applied to psychological topics.

Recognize and understand the impact of diversity on psychological research, theory and application, including (but not limited to): age, race, ethnicity, culture, gender, socio-economic status, disability, and sexual orientation.

rows.title: Introduction to Religious Studies
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: Read and critically evaluate primary sources in religious studies.

Respond critically, analytically, and/or synthetically to issues dealing with various theories (theories including, but not limited to: history, sociology, politics, psychology, philosophy and anthropology) within religious studies.
Apply issues and concerns arising in religious studies to contemporary experience.
objectives: Create and articulate a historical, cultural, and/or intellectual matrix within which the concerns and the questions of the discipline of religious studies can be placed.

Read and critically evaluate selected primary sources in religious studies, including but not limited to sacred texts, dialogues, aphorisms, essays, sermons, theological treatises, credal formulae, novels, short stories, and non-textual primary sources such as music and visual art forms.

Respond critically, analytically, and/or synthetically in writing to issues dealing with religious studies, including but not limited to the origin of religion, the function of religion, the expression of religion in literature, psychology, sociology, history, anthropology, and the arts, the relationships between and among religions, and an understanding and appreciation for suppressed or ignored voices within religious studies.
Apply the ideas and concepts in the discipline of religious studies to contemporary experience in its social, institutional, psychological, anthropological and/or political manifestations.

rows.title: Introduction to World Religions
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: Read and critically evaluate primary sources in world religions.
Respond critically, analytically, and/or synthetically to issues dealing with world religions.
Apply the concepts and issues from world religious traditions to contemporary experience.
objectives: Create and articulate a historical, cultural, and/or intellectual matrix within which the concerns and the questions of the discipline of religious studies can be placed.

Read and critically evaluate selected primary sources in religious studies (including but not limited to, sacred texts, dialogues, aphorisms, essays, sermons, theological treatises, credal formulae, novels, short stories, and non-textual primary sources such as music and visual art forms).

Respond critically, analytically, and/or synthetically in writing to issues dealing with world religions (including but not limited to the cultural manifestations of religions around the world, the relationships between and among religions, an analysis of the competing truth claims made by world religions, and an understanding and appreciation for suppressed or ignored voices within religious studies).

Apply the ideas and concepts in the discipline of religious studies, specifically as manifested in the study of world religions, to contemporary experience in its social, institutional, psychological, philosophical, and/or political manifestations.

rows.title: Magic, Witchcraft, and Religion
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Evaluate a variety of religious beliefs and practices across cultures.
Apply anthropological research methods and theoretical approaches to the analysis of religion, magic and witchcraft and their respective practices.
Analyze the interaction of belief systems and religious traditions, including magic and witchcraft with the physical and social environment.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Introduce the relationship between magic and witchcraft within religious belief systems and anthropological theory.
Provide a historical overview from past to present of the development of beliefs and practices associated with magic, witchcraft, and religion.
Examine the central myths, ideas and worldview of various cultural groups across the world.
Differentiate between the various roles of traditional religious specialists and how these operate within social systems.
Introduce primary sources relevant to the study of magic, witchcraft, and religion.

rows.title: Introduction to Islam
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Describe the historical context in which the Islamic faith was born and the influences on how the religion developed.
Demonstrate an understanding of the prophet Muhammad and key events in his life.
Demonstrate an understanding of the central beliefs and practices of Islam.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Define Islam and discuss Islam and Muslims using the religious studies methods and tools.
Recognize and challenge popular stereotypes and assumptions about Islam and Muslims, and consider one’s own biases about "normal" practices and values.
Describe the historical context in which the Islamic faith was born and the influences on how the religion developed.

Discuss the different stages of Muhammad’s revelation, its themes, and his roles as prophet, worship leader, head-of-state, military general, judge, counselor, family man, and the example to Muslims of a holy and virtuous life.
Identify the core differences between Sunnis and Shiites and discuss the subdivisions within these larger divisions.
Explain core concerns and interpretations of Islamic ethical conduct.
Describe core features of Sufism, including intense student-master relationship, distinctive devotional practices, and visceral spiritual experiences.

Analyze the diverse significance of Jihad, its relation to Islamic and ‘Western’ theories of just war, and the context and vision that such groups as al-Qaeda and Palestinian Islamic Jihad who carry out their acts of "terror" or "martyrdom operations."
Describe the diverse folk practices and beliefs of Muslims in various nations including festivities, prayer, healing, death rituals, use of talismans, and saint venerations.
Discuss the history of Muslims in the United States and the current demographics, special concerns, and challenges of Muslim Americans.
Use the study of divergent Muslim-majority countries and groups to evaluate whether Islam has been and is a liberative or oppressive force for women.

Discuss the diversity of modern Islamic movements, organizations, and thinkers, including pacifist, pluralistic, and service-oriented, militaristic, exclusive, and power-oriented perspectives, and their visions and approaches for a better country and world.
Identify Muslim centers, mosques, and organizations within their own communities and demonstrate competence in communicating with individuals from these groups.

rows.title: Classical Mythology
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:

Identify key members of the Olympic pantheon and their classical mythological contexts. 2. Identify key figures in mythology apart from the Olympian pantheon (Jason, Heracles, Homer, Achilles, etc.). 3. Analyze and write about a contemporary work that significantly references classical mythological elements by comparing and contrasting the work to the body of classical mythological texts studied in class.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Identify, compare, and contrast Greek and Roman gods and goddesses by identifying their appearance, associations, narratives, and characteristics.
Define key words used in discussions of classical mythology.
Recall and list key names and actions of major figures in classical mythology.
Differentiate between Greek and Roman treatments of mythological figures.
Relate mythological figures to their sources (i.e., authors or regional traditions).
Locate important mythological sites on a map of the classical world.
Recognize key dates in the history of classical civilization.
Define and describe various mythological creatures.
Identify significant characters and events in the Trojan War.
Compare and contrast differences between oral and literary traditions.
Describe typical events or steps in a generic hero's journey.
Identify mythological characters, events, or themes in later art, literature and film.
Evaluate the aesthetic merit of individual narratives.

rows.title: Jesus and His Interpreters
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: Read and critically evaluate primary sources with the study of Jesus and his interpreters.
Respond critically, analytically, and/or synthetically to issues within the study of the identities and interpretations of Jesus.
Relate the concepts and issues surrounding Jesus and his interpreters to contemporary experience.
objectives: Formulate and express a historical, cultural, and/or intellectual matrix within which the concerns and the questions regarding the so-called "historical Jesus" and the "Christs of faith" can be placed.

Read and critically evaluate selected primary sources related to the so-called "historical Jesus" and the "Christs of Faith" (including but not limited to Hebrew Scriptures [TANAK], the Christian Scriptures, intertestamental literature, both canonical and noncanonical, early Christian theological literature, Judeo-Christian historiography, non Judeo-Christian texts, as well as contemporary literature and the arts).

Respond critically, analytically, and/or synthetically in writing to recognize and understand the various identities and interpretations of Jesus from a multitude of sources, including suppressed and/or ignored voices throughout history (these sources may include, but not limited to the themes of historiography, hermeneutics, salvation history, symbolic language, and visual images of Jesus).
Apply the ideas and concepts in the area of interpretations of Jesus to contemporary experience.

rows.title: Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation:  Basic Life Support Healthcare Provider

Respond to choking emergencies
Describe the technique for relief of foreign body airway obstruction for an adult or child
Describe the technique for relief of foreign body airway obstruction for an infant

rows.title: Fundamentals and Mental Health
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Deliver safe, patient-centered, evidence-based nursing care to individuals and families across the lifespan in mental health and various healthcare settings.
Understand the vocational nurse's scope of practice, including a foundational understanding of ethical and legal principles in mental health and various healthcare settings.
Understand leadership principles in various health care settings, including mental health.
Recognize caring behaviors that support patient-centered care and interprofessional collaboration.
Develop effective communication skills for collaboration with the healthcare team to improve patient outcomes.
Demonstrate foundational clinical reasoning and clinical judgment necessary to provide safe patient care.
Understanding nursing informatics and technology to enhance patient care and decision-making.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Select and incorporate basic patient-centered interventions, in accordance with the care or treatment plan, that demonstrate sensitivity and respect for the diversity of the human experience.

Perform and document a basic fundamental assessment, for the purpose of data collection across the lifespan, including patient's experiencing alterations in mental health, encompassing values, preferences, expressed needs, and the impact of developmental, emotional, cultural, religious, and spiritual influences on the patient's health status.

Participate in the development of a patient-centered plan of care, using the nursing process and clinical judgment model, that addresses the psychosocial and physiological needs, including health promotion and maintenance, of patients within the health care system.
Safely prepare and administer medications, including the accurate calculation of drug dosages.
Demonstrate patient advocacy skills in the care of assigned patients and their families.
Develop a nursing philosophy statement that includes an individualized lifelong learning plan to prepare for becoming a competent, entry-level vocational nurse.

Establish professional attitudes and behaviors, including attention to appearance, demeanor, respect for self and others, and attention to professional boundaries with patients and families, as well as caregivers.
Understand and demonstrate professional standards, ethical behaviors, and legal principles of nursing practice.
Develop and use organizational and time management skills to safely manage the health care needs of assigned patients.
Demonstrate accountability and responsibility for nursing care provided and identify situations when care can be delegated to other healthcare team members.
Demonstrate relationship-centered care principles when caring for self and interacting with patients, families, peers, and other members of the health care team.
Identify and develop expected patient outcomes in a collaborative and caring manner that provides direction for continuity of care.
Select basic nursing interventions appropriate to the patient's developmental level; physical and psychosocial needs; spiritual beliefs; and culture.
Involve the patient and family when planning or providing patient- centered care in preparation for becoming a vocational nurse.
Identify and report relevant information to an appropriate interprofessional healthcare team member to improve patient outcomes.
Use and document basic patient care data to inform the interprofessional health care team and contribute to clinical decision-making.

Use effective communication and collaborative skills with the interprofessional health care team to deliver evidence-based patient-centered care.
Recognize the role of the vocational nurse in fostering collaborative relationships with the interprofessional health care team in improving patient outcomes.
Demonstrate effective communication techniques to foster positive professional working relationships.
Use quality improvement principles to identify potential problems that may interfere with the delivery of safe patient care.
Participate in guided self-reflection activities to identify professional learning needs.
Perform ongoing evaluation of expected outcomes and interventions and participate in the revision of the individualized plan of care as needed.

Use beginning clinical reasoning and judgment skills when providing quality, safe patient-centered care.

Use of information technology systems, at a foundational level, to prevent the risk of errors and improve clinical outcomes in the delivery of safe patient care.
